result:
I’ve been thinking lately about the texture of ordinary days—how they accumulate into a life almost without permission. The way morning light hits a particular wall in late October, and you notice it for the first time in years, or maybe ever. The small violence of a cabinet door left open. The particular silence of a room after someone you love has left it.

There’s something I keep returning to: the idea that we’re all living in the aftermath of futures we once imagined. The child who wanted to be an astronaut and now dreads spreadsheets. The teenager who wrote poetry in margins and now speaks in the flattened language of corporate email. Not tragic, exactly. Just—displaced. Haunted by versions of ourselves that never got to finish their sentences.

I find myself drawn to the unclaimed moments. The person eating alone at a diner at 2 AM, not because they’re lonely, but because the world feels more porous at that hour. The dog sleeping in a patch of sun, completely unbothered by the concept of wasted time. The elderly woman I saw once, in a grocery store parking lot, holding a cantaloupe to her ear like a seashell, shaking it, listening for something. I wanted to know what she heard. I wanted to know if she found it.

There’s a kind of writing I mistrust—the kind that rushes to meaning, that tidies up the mess of consciousness into a moral or a lesson. I prefer the mess. The sentence that starts in one direction and ends up somewhere else entirely, like a walk you take without a destination and suddenly you’re in a neighborhood you don’t recognize, and the not-knowing is the whole point.

I’ve been reading about mycelium networks, how trees communicate through roots, how a forest is less a collection of individuals than a single living conversation. I wonder if human connection works similarly—if we’re all just nodes in something vaster and slower than we can perceive, our small talk and our confessions both carrying nutrients or warnings across distances we can’t map.

Or maybe that’s just a pretty metaphor for loneliness. I’m never sure. I think the not-being-sure is also the point.

What I’m circling, I think, is attention. The rare and vanishing practice of actually looking at what is in front of you. Not to photograph it. Not to diagnose it. Not to mine it for content. Just to be present to the irreducible fact of it—a chipped mug, a stranger’s unusual laugh, the way rain makes asphalt darker and somehow more honest.

The world is always trying to sell us transcendence. Apps, retreats, transformations. But I’m increasingly suspicious of transcendence. Give me immanence. Give me the ground. Give me the courage to find the infinite in the thoroughly finite, the sacred in the stubbornly mundane.

I don’t know if this is wisdom or just exhaustion dressed up in philosophy. Probably both. Probably everything is several things at once, and our categories are just provisional shelters we build against the weather of complexity.

I’ll stop here, but not because I’m finished. Only because there’s a crow outside my window doing something interesting with a stick, and I want to watch.
